topic: Lightning vs the Sun: which is really hotter?
notes: 3 rounds, same units on both sides (degrees F or C, seconds): 1) surface heat: a lightning channel can reach ~50,000 F (NWS) vs the Sun's visible surface ~10,000 F (NASA) -> lightning, about 5x hotter; 2) how long: a flash lasts a fraction of a second vs the Sun shining for ~4.6 billion years -> Sun; 3) hottest point: lightning ~50,000 F vs the Sun's core ~27 million F -> Sun. Twist: the bolt beats the Sun's skin, but not its heart. Final 2-1 Sun. Fulgurite (sand fused to glass) as the visual proof of lightning heat. Sources to check: weather.gov/safety/lightning-temperature, NOAA SciJinks, NASA Sun facts (surface and core), Britannica. Plausibility 16/11: NWS and NASA give these figures. Hook (control, question): 'Lightning vs the Sun: which is hotter?' First second: a bolt flashing next to the Sun. Category science: rotation after tech (18/11; themed 21/11 does not count). Format versus: fewest reels once 18/11 (myth) and 21/11 (quiz) are out, tie with what_if, used longest ago (13/11).

topic: What if you had a dog's nose for one day?
notes: Grounded what_if, not scary. Premise: you wake up with a dog's nose (dogs have up to ~300 million olfactory receptors vs ~6 million in people, NOVA/PBS). First minute: breakfast smells as separate layers, not one smell; a dog could notice a teaspoon of sugar in a million gallons of water, about two Olympic pools (NOVA, Alexandra Horowitz). First hour: on a walk you smell in stereo (each nostril samples separately, so you know where a smell comes from) and the slits at the side of the nose push exhaled air away so sniffing never stops; you can 'smell time': an old trail smells weaker than a fresh one, so you know how long ago someone passed (Horowitz). Long term: the part of the brain that analyses smells is, proportionally, about 40x bigger in a dog (NOVA). What it teaches: a walk is your dog's newspaper, so let it sniff; twist: humans are not as bad as we think (McGann 2017, Science: human smell is a 19th-century myth; people can follow a chocolate scent trail on all fours, Porter et al. 2007). Say 'scientists estimate'; receptor counts vary by source and breed, keep 'up to'. Sources to check on the day: pbs.org/wgbh/nova/article/dogs-sense-of-smell, NOVA '6 stinking cool facts about dog noses', AKC 'The nose knows', McGann 2017 (Science), Porter 2007 (Nature Neuroscience). Plausibility 23/11: NOVA and AKC agree on the figures. Hook (control, question), max 10 words, e.g. 'What if you had a dog's nose for one day?'. First second: the young man sniffing with a big dog nose and smell trails flying in. Category nature: rotation after science (23/11). Format what_if: fewest reels in the log (2; the others have 3). 26/11 is Thanksgiving but the themed reel was already published 21/11 (reels: 1), so this is a regular reel. Closing: not cat_take (23/11); a light cat_take could fit but use real_life or bonus. Length standard (control): B2-length has no free slots.

topic: Why does a week have 7 days?
notes: Explainer: hook 'Why does a week have 7 days?' (question, control). Context: days, months and years follow the sky; the week does not. Steps: 1) the Babylonians watched seven moving lights (Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) and the Moon's phases change about every 7 days (a lunar cycle of ~29.5 days split in four); 2) the Jewish seven-day week with a day of rest spread it; the Romans (who used an 8-day market week, the nundinae) adopted the planetary week, and Emperor Constantine made it official in 321 AD; 3) the day names still carry the planets: Saturday = Saturn, Sunday = Sun, Monday = Moon (other languages keep more: Spanish martes = Mars). Surprising fact: France tried a 10-day week after the Revolution (1793) and dropped it by 1805; the Soviet Union tried 5- and 6-day weeks (1929-1940) and went back. Say 'historians think' where the origin is uncertain (the exact Babylonian link is debated); keep religion neutral and factual. Sources to check on the day: Britannica 'week', Astronomy.com 'Why are there 7 days in a week? Thank the Babylonians', Atlas Obscura 'Why can't we get rid of the 7-day week?', Almanac.com, webexhibits.org/calendars/week.html. Plausibility 23/11: Astronomy.com, Atlas Obscura and Almanac agree. Characters: reuse ancient_person (generic ancient tunic) as the sky-watcher, young_man with a calendar. Category history: rotation after nature (26/11). Format explainer: all other formats tie at 3 once 26/11 (what_if) is out; explainer used longest ago (goosebumps 30/10). Not the same format as 26/11. Length standard (control).
